name: Hans Hofmann
teaser: The German-American teacher who taught half of American abstract painting — his theory of 'push and pull' in color and his late slabs of bright geometry made him a key bridge from European modernism to the New York School.

exploreAction.targetName: The Gate (1960) or the late color compositions
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Hofmann makes colors advance and recede: a red square pushes toward you while a blue one pulls away — he called it 'push and pull.' His late works are like architecture made of color. He taught Lee Krasner and Helen Frankenthaler, among hundreds.

name: Adolph Gottlieb
teaser: The American painter of pictographs and suns — his early 'pictographs' put symbols in grids like cave paintings, and his later 'bursts' pair a glowing disk with violent black strokes. He was one of the first Abstract Expressionists and one of the most disciplined.

exploreAction.targetName: The Burst series or the pictographs
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a Burst: a red sun above, black marks below, the tension between them unspoken. Then look at his pictographs — grids of eyes, hands, and boats that feel ancient and immediate. Gottlieb said the artist's job is 'to create a world that mirrors the complexities of our own.'

name: Barnett Newman
teaser: The American painter of the zip — his huge canvases, each divided by one or two vertical lines of color, are among the most radical paintings of the century. He wanted the viewer to feel awe, standing before something like a void.

exploreAction.targetName: Vir Heroicus Sublimis (MoMA) — stand close
exploreAction.instruction: Stand close to this 8-foot-tall red field and let the zips pull your eye up and down. Newman said he wanted the viewer to feel 'as if they were looking at a thing for the first time.' He failed as a painter for decades, then changed everything.

name: Clyfford Still
teaser: The loneliest of the Abstract Expressionists — his jagged fields of black, red, and gold are like torn landscapes, painted by a man who refused to sell his work or explain it. He gave 800 paintings to a museum built just for him.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1948-49 canvases (Clyfford Still Museum, Denver)
exploreAction.instruction: Stand before the big canvases: fields of color with torn, lightning-shaped edges, as if the painting is flaking away from something underneath. Still called his work 'a humbling and ruthless quest.' No titles, no explanations — just the paintings, huge and unapologetic.

name: Robert Motherwell
teaser: The intellectual of Abstract Expressionism — his Elegy to the Spanish Republic series, with its black ovals and verticals, is a 40-year meditation on the Spanish Civil War and loss. He was also the movement's greatest writer and explainer.

exploreAction.targetName: Elegy to the Spanish Republic No. 34 (1954) — the ovals
exploreAction.instruction: Black forms hang like funeral bells between vertical bars on a white ground. Look at how the same shapes repeat across 150 versions — Motherwell painted one elegy his whole life. He said the series was 'a lullaby for the dead.'

name: Franz Kline
teaser: The American painter of black iron bridges — his huge black-and-white canvases look like calligraphy the size of buildings, giant strokes of a brush loaded with house paint. He found the style by projecting his small drawings onto a wall.

exploreAction.targetName: Chief (1950) or the black-and-white canvases
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the scale: Kline's strokes are so big they read as structures — beams, girders, fences — even though they're pure gesture. The story: a friend projected his sketches bigger and Kline saw their power. He painted like a bridge builder who only used black.

name: Philip Guston
teaser: The American painter who committed career suicide on purpose — after success as an abstract painter, he turned to lumpy cartoons of hoods, lightbulbs, and shoes that critics hated. Today those late paintings are considered among the most important of the century.

exploreAction.targetName: The Studio or the late hood paintings
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the hooded figures: Ku Klux Klan members driving, painting, smoking — painted as lumpy, cartoonish, and disturbingly human. Guston said 'I was always surprised that some people think of the Klan as an abstract symbol.' He painted himself into them. Honesty over comfort.

name: Milton Avery
teaser: The American painter who made color breathe — his flattened seascapes, figures, and interiors in big soft shapes influenced Rothko, Gottlieb, and a whole generation. He said he painted 'a suggestion of what I saw,' and the suggestion was sublime.

exploreAction.targetName: Sea Grasses and Blue Sea or the bathers
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Avery simplifies: a beach is four bands of color, a woman is a shape, a sea is blue stretched thin. Everything is reduced to its feeling. Rothko said Avery's work taught him about color's 'inner life.' Small paintings, enormous calm.

name: Arthur Dove
teaser: The first American abstract painter — he began making non-objective works in 1910, the same year as Kandinsky, and spent his life painting nature's rhythms: hills as waves, fog as color. He lived on a boat and painted from memory.

exploreAction.targetName: Fog Horns or the nature abstractions
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Fog Horns: two dark shapes and circles of sound — you can almost hear it. Dove abstracted from nature, not from theory: a field, a sound, a season, flattened into color and rhythm. He said he wanted to paint 'the sun's warmth in a hill.'

name: Marsden Hartley
teaser: The American painter of mountains and German military pageantry — he moved from Maine to Paris to Berlin, painted mystic German motifs in one decade and granite Maine peaks in another, and grieved openly in his art. He was a loner with a colossal color sense.

exploreAction.targetName: Mount Katahdin or the Portrait of a German Officer
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Portrait of a German Officer: a memorial made of badges, crosses, and flags — painted for his friend Karl von Freyburg, killed in WWI. Then Mount Katahdin: a raw, radiant mountain in gold and green. Hartley painted both grief and granite with the same fierce hand.

name: John Marin
teaser: The American watercolorist of Manhattan and Maine — his views of skyscrapers, boats, and the sea are built from explosive lines and washes that make buildings sway like ships. Alfred Stieglitz exhibited him for decades and called him a great American original.

exploreAction.targetName: Lower Manhattan or the Maine seascapes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Marin draws a skyscraper: crooked lines, flying watercolor, the building tilting like it's alive. He said he wanted to paint the city's 'movement and feeling,' not its facts. His Maine boats bob on seas of white paper. Energy, in watercolor.

name: Stuart Davis
teaser: The American painter who turned jazz into painting — his hard-edged compositions of gas stations, signs, and jazz clubs are full of bold words, stripes, and syncopated color. He said he painted what he heard.

exploreAction.targetName: The Mellow Pad or the jazz-inspired compositions
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the words: 'EVERY WHICH WAY,' 'RED BOX,' — Davis painted signs and sounds as flat shapes, arranged with a drummer's timing. His paintings swing. He was influenced by jazz, the French avant-garde, and American billboards, and he made them all one thing.

name: Charles Demuth
teaser: The American precisionist of flowers and factories — his I Saw the Figure 5 in Gold, inspired by a William Carlos Williams poem, is a masterpiece of typography and city light. He painted delicate watercolors of flowers and bold industrial scenes with equal love.

exploreAction.targetName: I Saw the Figure 5 in Gold (Met) — the number
exploreAction.instruction: A fire truck's number 5 blasts through concentric frames of gold, grey, and black — a poem made visible. Look at the layers: 'BILL,' 'CARLO,' the streetlights. Demuth translated Williams's poem about a fire engine into pure graphic power. Poetry and paint, welded.

name: Elie Nadelman
teaser: The Polish-American sculptor who made elegant figures from a few curved lines — his circus performers, dancers, and society women are built like notes of music in marble and wood. He said sculpture should be 'the study of pure form.'

exploreAction.targetName: The Man in the Top Hat or the circus figures
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Nadelman reduces a figure to arcs: a top hat is a curve, a coat is another, the whole body a chord of circles. His art is folk and classical at once. He lost his fortune in 1929 and kept making his elegant, lonely figures anyway.

name: Gaston Lachaise
teaser: The French-American sculptor of the monumental woman — his Standing Woman is a goddess of bronze with swelling hips and outstretched arms, the opposite of every skinny ideal. He sculpted the same woman (his wife Isabel) for forty years.

exploreAction.targetName: Standing Woman (1912-27) — walk around it
exploreAction.instruction: Walk around the bronze goddess: from every side she swells and tilts differently. Lachaise said he met Isabel as a young man and 'the world changed' — he sculpted her glory for the rest of his life. Big, generous, and unapologetic.

name: Alexander Calder
teaser: The American sculptor who invented the mobile — his hanging constructions of painted metal balance and sway with the air, turning sculpture into choreography. He also made the giant stabile sculptures that guard plazas worldwide.

exploreAction.targetName: A mobile (MoMA or Tate) — watch it move
exploreAction.instruction: Stand still and watch: the mobile turns imperceptibly, red and black disks finding new balances. Calder said he wanted art 'to move, to have motion.' He was an engineer first; his toys and circus were his training. Air is his collaborator.

name: David Smith
teaser: The American sculptor of welded steel who built monuments out of found metal — his Cubi series stacks gleaming stainless-steel boxes into heroic totems. He worked like a painter, arranging forms on his property in upstate New York.

exploreAction.targetName: The Cubi series — the steel
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Smith balances stacked steel boxes: they seem to defy gravity, polished so they catch the sky. He said he drew with steel. He died in a car crash at 59, and his late works made him the most influential American sculptor of the 20th century.

name: Isamu Noguchi
teaser: The Japanese-American sculptor who made gardens, lamps, and furniture into sculpture — his Akari paper lanterns, his playground designs, and his stone garden in Paris are calm objects with cosmic ambitions. He spent a WWII internment camp year, then built peace in stone.

exploreAction.targetName: The UNESCO Peace Garden (Paris) or the Akari lamps
exploreAction.instruction: Walk through the UNESCO garden: rocks, water, and silence arranged so the city disappears. Then look at an Akari lamp: a paper shade that glows like a moon. Noguchi said sculpture should be 'a thing to sit in, a garden to walk through.' He made space his material.

name: Louise Nevelson
teaser: The American sculptor of black wooden walls — she filled boxes with chair legs, banisters, and scraps, painted them all black (or gold or white), and stacked them into silent, monumental cities. She began exhibiting seriously in her 60s.

exploreAction.targetName: Sky Cathedral (MoMA) — the wall
exploreAction.instruction: Stand back: the wall of boxes reads as one dark, rhythmical building. Step close: every compartment holds a found object — a finial, a doorknob, a wheel. Nevelson painted everything one color to make the shadows the real sculpture. She called black 'the most aristocratic color of all.'

name: Chaim Gross
teaser: The Austrian-American sculptor of acrobats and dancers — his carved wooden figures of women in motion are among the most joyful sculptures of the century. He learned carving in Vienna, escaped the Holocaust, and filled New York with leaping figures.

exploreAction.targetName: The acrobat and dancer sculptures
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Gross carves a contortionist: the body bends through the wood, limbs interlocking, the grain becoming muscle. He worked directly in wood with chisels, no models. His figures tumble and balance with a circus joy that never dims.

name: Hugo Robus
teaser: The American sculptor of smooth, simplified figures — his women combing hair, dancing, and daydreaming are polished into soft, timeless volumes. He waited decades for recognition, then saw a solo show at the Whitney at 77.

exploreAction.targetName: Girl Washing Her Hair or the dancers
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the surfaces: Robus polished his bronze figures until they feel like wet stone. His subjects are everyday — a woman washing her hair, a dancer mid-turn — but the forms are eternal. Patience was his medium; his late fame was his reward.
